newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia, China set date for rights talks.
newsitem.headline: Australia, China set date for rights talks.

text.p: Australia and China will begin an unprecedented dialogue on human rights in August, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Tuesday.
The human rights dialogue, the communist nation's first such bilateral forum, will begin in Beijing, Downer said after a meeting in Canberra with Chinese Vice-Premier Zhu Rongji.

"The first round of this process will begin in August of this year, so we've got it up and running very quickly, and a range of different human rights issues that are of concern to us will naturally enough be pursued in the context of that dialogue," Downer said.
Australia and China agreed in April to establish the formal dialogue on human rights but set no starting date.
The conservative Australian government says such a dialogue is the only way it can achieve an improvement in China's human rights performance.

"We have some optimism that taking this difficult aspect of the relationship and managing it in the way we're proposing to manage it and the positive response we've got so far from China on this difficult and sensitive question of human rights is a significant advance from the position Australia has had for quite some years," Downer said.

The agreement follows a recent warming in the two countries' relations, which worsened in a series of diplomatic and security spats following the Liberal-National coalition's election victory in March 1996.
Downer said the Chinese leader had allayed Canberra's concerns that Beijing might view Australia's recent strengthening of relations with the United States as a move to contain China.
The government-run China Daily newspaper revived those concerns on Monday in a long opinion piece attacking Australia's defence links with the United States.
"We raised with the vice-premier the article that had appeared in the China Daily and...he said that neither the Chinese government nor China's leaders thought that way," Downer said.
"So we're very pleased that the views that were expressed in that article are not views that are shared by the leadership of China," he said.

During the talks, Zhu also said China would buy more wool from Australia, while reducing the tariff barriers facing Australian wool exporters. But the two had not discussed the quantity of wool to be bought or the amount of tariff reduction.
China has imposed tariffs of 15 percent on wool imports.
China is Australia's largest wool export market, with sales worth A$665 million (US$512 million) in the year to June 1996.
